This, Mr. Speaker, is the testimony of an American economist who thinks it possible to democratize money and to use new interest-free credit for the development and social organization of a country.
While the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and this government allow rises in the interest rate and increase the burden of the Canadian taxpayer, everywhere in the world loans are granted under extremely easy conditions, $25, $30, $50 and even $100 million interest-free loans for periods of time from 50 to 60 years and often with a 10 years' grace period.
Those who are against Social Credit generally claim that the application of Creditiste theories would lead to inflation. The Liberal members said it, the Conservative members agree and, unfortunately, a number of economists who base their studies upon the data of the present system, think so too.
However, it is to be noticed that in Canada as well as in the United States, both countries, like most countries in the world, are facing this kind of malaise that they call "inflation" and which was brought about by the unbalanced financial system of today. Is it the fault of the social credit, a doctrine which is not applied anywhere, or is it the fault of the actual financial system?
Today, there is no shortage of credit. The problem is that the credit is not social enough. In these days, it is not necessary to be an expert to find the great number of credit facilities available to the people.
Federal and provincial governments give us a great many examples of the way credit is used in all departments. Such a procedure has become normal. We find that at times, during the session of the various legislatures, federal or provincial, discussions become animated when estimates have to be approved or rejected.
The minister concerned sometimes becomes nervous and anxious. He feels the need to call upon the best advisers in his department to help him justify the use of the estimates submitted for approval. This occasional tension is due to misuse of certain credits voted to cover expenses that sometimes greatly exceed the experts' estimations, because they failed to take probable waste into consideration.
The Glassco report demonstrated how bureaucrats can disrupt the experts' forecasts when carelessness prevails constantly in economic fields where efficiency should be the rule.
June 15, 1970

Suggested Interest-free Loans
In addition to the kind of credit we have been discussing, there are many others: international, national, provincial, municipal, import, export, credit for purchasing, credit for sales. Indeed our country has advanced so much in the field of credit under our present financial system that we grant credit to foreign countries for the purchase of our products.
Here in Canada, many Canadians are bom, live and die on credit. People are continually in tow of the publicity heard on television or radio. A lot of them are feeding themselves with instant products, three minutes meals, and are relying on automatic machines bought on credit. All those rogues have helped many families get head over ears in debt.
But, we need not loose heart, our credit is still good with the finance companies which will provide us with the credit we need to balance our budget for the time being. It is even possible to purchase on credit a secondhand car at the cheapest possible price, in spite of all the hazards this implies in terms of highway safety.
However, the whole process by which these various terms and conditions of credit are established is directed, controlled, managed and monopolized by the system which issues bank credit.
Things controlled by man are subject to the human laws of production, exchange and purchasing power. This power is expressed in a practical way by monetary values. Money is to the exchange of goods what words are to the exchange of ideas. Production and consumption are thus related to the purchasing power or to the exchange power.
If we consider the world as a whole, we realize there is a blockage, an obstruction. For instance, the farming people in Canada are seriously threatened by overproduction due to deviation of consumption. The accumulated surpluses of Canadian wheat are equivalent to eight years of consumption. The dairy products of Canada are anxiously waiting for consumers. In 1969, overproduction of milk in Canada reached one billion pounds of milk or 100 million gallons. Lawyers have now come to the point where they are inverting the order of creation by saying to the farm producers:	"Stop sowing; kill your
cows."
A premium of $200 is about to be granted to the milk producers in six countries of the Common Market for every milk cow slaughtered.

Too poor to buy their own products, Canadians eat imported foods and chemical products sold at bargain prices. While underfed people are lacking milk and wheat, Canadian citizens, surrounded by mountains of wheat and heaps of milk cans, are suffering from hunger and from thirst.
Capitalis, the object of which is to regularize means of exchange is therefore in a bad conditoin. It should be corrected but not destroyed.
Instead of laying our economic system upon logical principles, upon the natural pattern, we remain tied to a system which does not provide the necessary means of distributing the existing abundance. Thus thousands of Canadian citizens must live in slums while there are enormous quantities of building materials available for the building of decent homes.
Thousands of Canadian citizens have to resort to social relief so as not to suffer too much from hunger, in a country offering through all possible advertising means such a great variety of products. Macaulay wrote in "The History of England":
The stability of the modem world is based upon the stability of its money, but it is obvious that the value of currency is unstable.
Whether all hardships inflicted upon the British people by bad kings, bad Parliaments, bad ministers and bad judges are not equal to the hardships due to the poor currency is doubtful-
A sound currency, namely a currency that keeps its stability through the repayment of debts and its purchasing power and which protects the purchasing power of salaries, savings and pensions, is the key to economic freedom, to progress and to development.
The end and objective of a monetary policy are therefore to maintain the dollar stability and to be the instrument of a maximum production. Indeed, next to the maintenance of law and order in a country, that should be the greatest responsibility of the state.
Everybody admits that the value of currency is based on goods and services. A steady balance should however be provided between the money issued and the production of goods.
It is unbelievable that governments, one after another, should have allowed private banks to create and issue millions of dollars in new currency without any obligation on their part of maintaining the stability of the purchasing power.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
We do not want to disrupt everything or to set up a printing-shop, as some simple-mind-
June 15, 1970

ed persons have suggested. We already have the institutions required. It is only a matter of adjusting the values, a matter of accounting, so that the financial machinery may reflect the actual wealth, taking into account human self-respect and the value of things that can be produced in large enough quantities to feed, house and clothe the whole population.
It is quite astonishing to realize that all those researchers, more especially in the economic field, have not managed to come up with some means of distributing the abundant production that only has to be oriented to meet the needs of those waiting for it. There is certainly no shortage of means of transportation, since we have reached the point of going to the moon, spending millions of dollars just to satisfy our curiosity to "peer" on another planet, when thousands of human beings suffer from hunger, lack of shelter, clothing and care.
It is high time that our politicians, now at the helm, find a solution other then the plans submitted until now and which have only favoured even more the rich at the expense of the poor.
We do not pretend that the Social Credit theory we are advocating will be a panacea but it is logical to forecast that it will eliminate many reasons for concern.

That is a great example of social credit: you find yourself abandoned, without friends. That is where the taxpayers of Alberta find themselves, abandoned and without friends.
Social Credit is supposed to be a free enterprise party. It is supposed to support the taxpayers, the people who do the work. But have those who do the work in Alberta benefited? I will speak for myself. In a small town of 3,500 people, which has no university, my taxes are $700 per year on a three-bedroom house. From the provincial government I get $50 rebate, so my full taxes are $650. If the Social Crediters are sincere, why do they not put oil revenues at the disposal of the municipalities? With considerable riches, hundreds of millions of dollars a year coming in, why do they not put some of this money at the disposal of the people who need it most, the bankrupt municipalities?
Mr. Speaker, if you examine the record you will find that the municipalities in the rich province of Alberta are the worst off in Canada. I can only come to one conclusion, that the Social Crediters do not mean or practice what they preach. They have the money in Alberta. They do not have to go to New York for it. It is there in Alberta, but the municipalities cannot get it because the Social Crediters want the same old power that most governments want, the power to control the purse strings and never mind the poor little worker, the poor little taxpayer. How long do you think you can go on killing the goose that lays the golden egg? Not much longer.

We in the Conservative party have been consistent throughout the years. Taking over in 1957, we found the country bankrupt as it is today. We found the people of Canada starving in the midst of plenty. We found them with too much grain, too many cattle, too many hogs, too many chickens and nobody to buy these things. So we adopted the only answer-not a quick answer, and not a sharpened pencil. We adopted a rolled-up sleeves, back to work, back to trading policy and we balanced the country's budgets. We got the economy rolling. The only sorrow of Canadians is that they allowed the same old gang to take over again and put us back where we were 13 sad years ago.
We must go back to work in order to compete in the markets of the world. We have efficiency in the working people of Canada. This is no class war that I am waging. In this context I mean the people who are producing, the small businessman, the manufacturer, the efficient builder of houses and the entrepreneur. They are the real source of wealth in this country and no government has a right to tax them, no government has a right to lay red herrings across the trail-Socialist red herrings or Social Credit red herrings- because only through hard work, with reasonable prices and solid world markets, can we regain our feet.
Solid world markets made success possible for us, after we were forced to devalue the dollar, not because of any fault of ours but because Canada was bankrupt. We took the only way out. We got back into the export markets of the world. We recovered our share of the export markets and we sold every bushel of grain until the boast of the Minister of Agriculture of that day was, "You grow it; we will sell it." It is a long time since anybody has dared to say that about agriculture or any other sector of the economy, except perhaps nickel, uranium and some of the other hardware of war.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
No government has ever been proud that the only way Canada could keep afloat was to supply the world with war materials. You are getting this from a self-declared hawk, Mr. Speaker. I am a hawk to the extent that I believe in the full defence of Canada. I find it passing strange, Mr. Speaker, that anybody would dare pretend that an experiment like this would work, for 25 years when they have had the finest opportunity, in the richest province in Canada, to put it into effect and nothing has been done but to give a $20 bill. That is all the people of Alberta ever got. This scheme is a dead loss; it would not even pay the interest on $25 a month for one year. For the last 20 years I have been hearing this empty nonsense, and I am tired of it. If the Social Crediters of Canada would only take a good look at the facts, they would realize that the only effective action in this situation is for all of us to get together with good, old-fashioned common sense, old-fashioned hard work and old-fashioned effort to retrieve the export markets of the world and compete with western Europe, the United States and Asia. We can show that the people of Canada have been, are now and always will be efficient.

The new doctrine of something for nothing, by right, is a lie. The people of Canada may want to give something out of the goodness of their hearts-they have done it to the extent of hundreds of millions of dollars-but there is nothing that says anybody has a right to it. No government has the right to take my charitable feelings and put them into print.
If we want to produce in this country an atmosphere in which a man can work, instead of taking away more and more of the profits of his labour we should be striving to give him more and more in his pay cheque for the work he performs. If you did this you would have fewer and fewer people needing relief. We need policies to send young people back to school. We need aggressive trade policies to sell goods in the markets of the world. We need to encourage businessmen. Forget the white paper and give the businessmen of Canada encouragement to compete in the markets of the world. They have to compete with manufactured goods in the way we have competed with agricultural products.
There is no more efficient farmer in the world than the Canadian farmer, but never has he been so hard up. The policy of lending interest-free money, money at 5 per cent, or subsidizing loans to farmers of western Canada will not do much good unless markets are found for their products. You are only hanging a debt around the farmer's neck. Why let him have $75,000 without a well-thought out policy on how he will pay it back? There is no such thing as debt-free money, and I would never vote for it.
My friends opposite voted for debt-free money. I do not know why they have had this sensible change of heart, except that they know it was Conservative policy which put Canada back on her feet between 1957 and 1962. To the extent that this administration has followed the guidelines we gave them, we have prospered. When they have gone off into the wild blue yonder on a wild goose chase, we have come to disaster. It is the people of Canada who have paid and who will pay until we return to the common sense of hard work, thrift and obtaining foreign markets.

Mr. Speaker, as I listened to the hon. member who spoke before me deal with the motion, I was under the impression that I was sitting in the Edmonton legislature in view of the efforts made to criticize the policy of the provincial government of Alberta. However, the motion is clear and it does say:
That, in view of the government's inability to effectively combat the frightening increase in the public debt in the opinion of this house, the public sector of the Canadian economy, including the federal government, the provinces, the municipalities and the schoolboards should be financed by interest free loans-
This is where there is a lack of objectivity and efforts are made to impute motives to the Ralliement creditiste and its supporters when they defend this policy.
In my estimation, a man who earns $100 and who agrees to lend it to a friend or a partner is really entitled to receive an interest because in some way he rents out the fruit of his labour. We recognize this and we accept it right away and I consider dishonest those who would like to make the people believe that we object to all this lending system of the fruit of one's work to an industry or to a chum. What we want especially is to lighten the burden of the individuals and the community by strongly urging the government so that all new credit based on the work, of all the Canadian people, be loaned to the federal government, the municipalities, the provinces, under an accounting system but free of interest which crushes everyone at the same time.
Last year, during a debate on pieces of legislation introduced by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) with regard to the Farm Credit Corporation,-to unfreeze this interest system which was frozen at 5 per cent,-our friends in the official opposition categorically objected to it arguing that it would tend to impose an extra burden on the farmers and place them in an unfavourable position.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if excessively high interest rates can create problems for private enterprise, for individuals, why should it be different in the case of the interests that crush the federal and provincial governments, all our public bodies, and those who administer them, who of necessity have to levy high enough taxes to meet their payments?
June 15, 1970

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I also thank my colleagues. I am convinced of one thing and it is that all of us here are working in all goodwill. We want our discussions to bring about improvements.
That is why the hon. member for Bellechasse was allowed to proceed with his remarks and he will not take advantage of the confidence and the right to speak granted to him.

I shall conclude my remarks and make my point by referring to a conference on pollution which I recently attended in France. I hope I may be allowed this reference for I believe that when parliament pays the expenses of members like the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau) or any other, for that matter, in order to make a trip, it is with a useful purpose in view.
We have studied there the problem of air and water pollution now facing mankind. The problem of providing us with fresh air is indeed important. I made a personal experience with a little bird. I tried to put it in a cage which I gradually made smaller, which means that the volume of oxygen was shrinking gradually, and I reduced its size to the extent where at one point, the bird flapped its wings, and dropped dead. Why? It had run out of air; there was an abundance of it around, but I controlled it.
We have also studied the important problem of water pollution. The problem is vital for the nations.
But there is another problem, that of the pollution of our financial system and of our democracy. We are polluted and do not realize it. We realize there is uneasiness, that some people are unhappy. We seek the cause, but we really avoid looking for it where it really lies. What is lacking? What is wrong? Those who oppose the reforms advocated by the Creditistes, embroil matters purposely. It is easy to do so, to ascribe all kinds of intentions to us.
But God knows that our intentions are as good as anyone else's. In Parliament and elsewhere, we want our work to be of benefit not only to ourselves but to others.
A while ago, I heard the hon. member from Pembina (Mr. Bigg) say that there are surpluses, and perhaps if we were to relax credit, this would create a surplus of money, which could become dangerous.
Allow me one small remark, no harm meant.
There are milk and wheat surpluses. But there are hungry people, deprived of the bare necessaries to whom we must bring relief and comfort.
Some people claim that all the Creditistes want is the recognition of rights but that they refuse to accept the obligations of community life. Nothing is further from the truth. We recognize that each individual has rights and obligations and that we cannot live within a
June 15, 1970

community if our rights and obligations are not respected. That is the reason why we keep saying that we must not only ensure the recognition of the rights of the individuals but also enable them to fulfil their moral, economic and social obligations. Why is it that so many people nowadays refuse to fulfil their obligations, within society? Because they are deprived of the right to participate through their work in the development of the community. I am shocked, as a head of family, to see that the Canadian government is spending in Sainte-Anne-Des-Plaines $32,450 per inmate. An institution was built to accommodate 450 inmates, while families, are systematically refused the right to obtain the credit required to build a home for their children.
In my opinion, the government is not living with the times when it does not make use of all possible means to ensure to these families a right to live in a dwelling of their choice large enough so that they might perpetuate the human race.
In France we were told that the French people do not wish to emigrate to Canada because they like to stay in their country. As for us who enjoy a huge country, we can increase our population in a natural way without being obliged to resort to integration as of birth into a given area, which would systematically allow the normal growth of the population because of the famous dollar which, coming from a system proposed by the Creditistes, will be inflationary, painful and bad because there will be too much money in circulation. However, if the money comes from those who control the credit of the nation without any active and industrious participation, it is not inflationary, or dangerous for the economy. This system is sacred, it must not be changed.
Therefore, let us continue to see things unrealistically.
Very few members know the tragic events which I and certain others lived through during the 1930-39 depression. We were not even allowed to have a 3-cent stamp to mail a letter to our mothers, and that really hurt. It is difficult to wait for daybreak at the edge of the wood to begin working without fear of injury. Some are laughing at that. Let them. He laughs longest who laughs last.
I have lived through such incidents and through those difficult years and today I consider it my duty, because I have been trained to fulfil my own responsibilities, to stand as

Parliament is supposed to group the best brains of a country, honest citizens who are supposed to work only for the nation and to develop the full physical, moral, intellectual and financial possibilities of a country. But any talk of reviewing our system, of correcting its inherent abuses is called nonsense.
Just while ago, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cote) stated that Liberals, Conservatives and NDP members disagreed with those who advocate an inflationary policy, a social, normal and intelligent policy which was only second-rate and extolled by a few members in a certain corner on the house who do not know what they are talking about. Those are approximately the words used by the minister.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
When we have ministers who do not even know the difference between public and private capital, how can the administration of a country be normal, consistent and beneficial to the people?
We are convinced that the public debt is a nonsense, that it is the worst monster which we ever had to face, a dreadful monster, with all the necessary power and tentacles to pick up all that is consistent, powerful and weighty: finance. And it is that monster which is protected by those who govern us in Canada since confederation.
It is the Liberals and the Conservatives who governed us. They are those who increased the public debt to please, to enrich, to give more strength to that monster which now crushes and chokes the whole population. And they too are being choked and crushed by that monster but, alas, they do not feel it!
It is a bit of luck for the House to have Ralliement creditiste members, who see things clearly, who have studied the situation and tell it like it is. Truly, the House should realize its luck in having us here.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) if he would reconsider his decision and take abortion out of the Criminal Code, thus freeing qualified doctors to act in consultation with
8146	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion pregnant women. He replied that both he and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has already stated the government position, and added, "that is it for the moment".
Last night in Vancouver the Prime Minister held what the Canadian Press terms "a reasonably orderly discussion" on the subject with about 60 members of the Women's Liberation Group. According to the press dispatch, the Prime Minister said that current laws allow doctors to perform abortions if they wish, but added that the liberalization proposed by the group would force them to do so, possibly against their will. No one knows better than the Prime Minister what the present abortion laws permit. He knows that they do not permit doctors to perform abortions, no matter how much they wish to do so, except under conditions so rigid that it is estimated that about one woman in every 500 who require an abortion can get one.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
As to the Prime Minister's charge that the changes proposed by the Women's Liberation Group would force doctors to perform abortions, possibly against their will, if the Prime Minister had taken the trouble to meet the group when they came to Ottawa on May 9, or even to read their brief, he would have seen that their demand in regard to abortion was simply this:
That in this session of Parliament the government sponsor a bill removing all mention of abortion from the Criminal Code.
There is no mention there, or anywhere else in the brief, of forcing doctors to perform abortions. Indeed, what the doctors need is freedom to follow their consciences, without the legal shackles of hospital boards and whole desert areas where there are not any hospitals that will permit abortions or where hospital facilities of any kind simply do not exist.
The truth is that our present abortion laws are forcing women to bear children regardless of their wishes, regardless of their state of health, regardless of whether or not they can afford to care for and educate them properly, regardless of what additional children do to the health and chances in life of the others. A few doctors, unable to watch the helpless misery of such women trapped by unwanted pregnancy, have been performing abortions on their own. With what result? They are arrested and tried as criminals. Last week

DEBATES	June 15, 1970
this happened to a respected doctor in Montreal, Dr. Henry Morgentaler, president of the Humanist Association of Canada. At a press conference in Ottawa he told of one woman, the mother of three children, brought into a Montreal hospital following a botched operation by a non-doctor. Infection developed and an emergency hysterectomy was performed, but several days after that press conference the woman died horribly of gas gangrene. No, Mr. Prime Minister, the current law does not permit doctors to perform abortions if they wish.
The Prime Minister is to be commended for trying to broaden the abortion laws last year in the face of strong opposition. But it is now evident that further changes are urgent to combat the menace of dangerous abortions performed by quacks and butchers and to wipe out the discrimination that permits a woman with means to have a safe abortion while a woman without money faces the risk of infection and death. The Prime Minister claims the public is not ready for changes in the abortion laws. A Gallup poll was taken in March of this year on the question, "Would you vote for a law that would permit a woman to terminate pregnancy at any time during the first three months?" Forty-three per cent said yes, 48 per cent said no, and 9 per cent were undecided.
A year ago it was the persistence and drive of the Prime Minister that put through the present abortion law. He did this in the face of opposition that would have discouraged most men in his position. I am quite convinced that if he now decides to make the change that experience has shown is necessary, that is, to take abortion out of the Criminal Code and leave the decision to the doctor and his patient, he will be able to switch that undecided 9 per cent into the "yes" column, thus making a safe majority of public opinion in favour of the change. Mr. Speaker, I hope the Prime Minister will take this risk as he took the risk to his career last year.
